subject: Posterior uncertainty estimation for gaussian processes with non-gaussian observation models

messages.author: d8b8f07888753155
messages.subject: Posterior uncertainty estimation for gaussian processes with non-gaussian observation models
parts:
Given many (10k+) series of observations of different candidates over times 1:t, I want to estimate what value I should expect at t+1 for any candidate. 
I will select the 100 candidates with the highest expectation for a future purpose, and so I will need to shrink the expected values for the selected series back towards the mean for all series in order to get an accurate revised expectation for these selected candidates.

I'm thinking to model this in 2 steps using 
1) gaussian processes to estimate the initial expectation for time t+1 and its uncertainty; and then subsequently
2) a gaussian mixture model for the distribution of true expectations, connected to the initial expectations from the previous step by the uncertainty from the previous step. This is a conventional hierarchical bayesian model.

My problem lies in estimating the uncertainty for the gaussian processes at t+1, which is crucial to an accurate Bayesian shrinkage in the next step. In particular, I'm sure that the observation model for the candidate series (the noise around the observations) is not gaussian, it's heavily left skewed. What I need is a way of modelling a skewed non-gaussian observation model while maintaining good Bayesian accounting for uncertainty in parameters & hyperparameters.

Flaxman, Gelman et al. in "Fast hierarchical Gaussian processes" using Stan, discuss "Extensions to non-Gaussian observation models", They end with the ominous words "In practice, we have had difficulties using HMC to update both z1, . . . , zn and the hyperparameters simultaneously. A reasonable solution might be to follow the blocked approach of [1, 32], wherein the hyperparameters are sampled with, e.g. HMC and then conditional on these hyperparameters the zi are sampled, with HMC or another algorithm." 

This sounds to me like they're saying that it doesn't really work to estimate hyperparameters in Stan when using non-Gaussian models, try GPStuff instead. However, GPstuff doesn't seem to allow for skewed likelihoods (although there is a log transform of observations in one of their examples. GPML, the other main package, has a warped Gaussian likelihood model available which is perfect, but does not appear to do proper Bayesian estimates of uncertainty including the uncertainty deriving from the hyperparameters.

Have I understood this all right? 
How much does mis-specification of the observation model effect posterior uncertainty anyway?
Is there a way to get where I need to go using Stan?
If not Stan, where else?

I'm happy to put the work into generating a case study for the Stan site, if someone could guide me in this jungle.

thanks for reading,

Jonathan

messages.author: f13fe7e880ed6103
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Posterior uncertainty estimation for gaussian processes with non-gaussian observation models
parts:
Sorry to be ominous. ;)

I'm sure Aki can tell you whether GPstuff has what you're looking for.
(http://arxiv.org/pdf/1206.5754.pdf lists a number of likelihoods that
might be useful, including Gaussian scale mixture and Student-t...)

But you might be okay in Stan, as there've been some improvements on
the backend since we wrote that paper, and many more are slated for
the future. Plus there's ADVI. Also, see the other discussion started
by Rachael in which we discuss various compromises / informative
priors which might help in the short term. Inducing points or random
fourier Features (which I have an implementation of in Stan that's
almost ready to share, but have also had issues with learning
hyperparameters) might also help.

A key question: how large is t? Am I right that you're imagining a
single GP prior from which all of the series of observations are
drawn?

Seth

messages.subject: Re: Posterior uncertainty estimation for gaussian processes with non-gaussian observation models
parts:
On Wednesday, March 23, 2016 at 9:15:10 PM UTC+2, Jonathan Shaw wrote:
This sounds to me like they're saying that it doesn't really work to estimate hyperparameters in Stan when using non-Gaussian models, try GPStuff instead. However, GPstuff doesn't seem to allow for skewed likelihoods (although there is a log transform of observations in one of their examples.

GPstuff has several observation models for skewed data (and usually it's so easy to add new ones that we can add what you need if you ask nicely). It's hard to recommend one of them or comment if you need something else based on just the information "skewed". Could you tell more about your data? It would be also helpful to know magnitude of t as it also has an effect on speed of GPs. You can also email if you want more help with GPstuff, as it is off-topic for this forum.
How much does mis-specification of the observation model effect posterior uncertainty anyway?
It depends on the amount of mis-specification :)
Is there a way to get where I need to go using Stan?

Probably not yet for 10k+ candidates, unknown t and non-Gaussian observation model. Hopefully in the future.

Aki

If not Stan, where else?

I'm happy to put the work into generating a case study for the Stan site, if someone could guide me in this jungle.

thanks for reading,

Jonathan

messages.author: d8b8f07888753155
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Posterior uncertainty estimation for gaussian processes with non-gaussian observation models
parts:
Many thanks for the replies Aki & Seth.

t (the number of values in series) will typically be around 2000 but could in some applications be 10000.
Each series will be a separate process, I'm not thinking one GP behind all the series.
The observation model will vary for each series, but a typical case might look roughly like a skew-normal gaussian with a mean of 5, a mode around -5, virtually nothing below -20, little weight above +20, but a long light tail stretching up to +500.

I'm attracted to seeing the observation model as being a mixture of 2 skew normal gaussians, with the mixing proportion as being the latent variable that evolves over time. This should be flexible enough to match the distributions of observations in any series well, and prior knowledge suggests that's it's not a bad picture for the physical reality underlying.

A comment of Andrew's on another GP thread pointed me towards time series models as a simpler alternative to GPs. Therefore I'm thinking that what I should do is start by implementing a time series approach, estimating the parameters of this skewnormal mixture, the fluctuation of the mixing proportion over time, and the resulting expectation and uncertainty at t+1.

Once I have this working I can see whether there is need to upgrade to using GPs. I'm thinking that because 
a) I have many data points, 
b) I am interested in a single process that evolves relatively slowly over time, and 
c) I only want to do inference relatively near my data
it might not be worth paying the price in time and complexity to upgrade to GP.

Does this seem like a sensible approach, considering what I want and the computational issues using Stan?

Many thanks again!

Jonathan

messages.author: f13fe7e880ed6103
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Posterior uncertainty estimation for gaussian processes with non-gaussian observation models
parts:
This all sounds sensible to me, especially given the scale of the
data. You could always take a small subset of the data and see how a
GP fit compares to a time series fit in terms of predicting t+1.

Re: "each series is a separate process." This sounds like "no
pooling." But if your data lends itself to it (do you have groups of
some kind?), you might consider partial pooling (hierarchical
structure) on the parameters you'll be estimating for the time series
model.

Seth

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Posterior uncertainty estimation for gaussian processes with non-gaussian observation models
parts:
On Thursday, March 24, 2016 at 2:34:24 PM UTC+2, Jonathan Shaw wrote:
t (the number of values in series) will typically be around 2000 but could in some applications be 10000.
10k+ independent models with t=2k-10k means that you need to consider the computational speed of alternative approaches.

Each series will be a separate process, I'm not thinking one GP behind all the series.
The observation model will vary for each series, but a typical case might look roughly like a skew-normal gaussian with a mean of 5, a mode around -5, virtually nothing below -20, little weight above +20, but a long light tail stretching up to +500.

I'm attracted to seeing the observation model as being a mixture of 2 skew normal gaussians, with the mixing proportion as being the latent variable that evolves over time. This should be flexible enough to match the distributions of observations in any series well, and prior knowledge suggests that's it's not a bad picture for the physical reality underlying.
Do you want the variance and skewness of the skew normal to evolve in time, too?
A comment of Andrew's on another GP thread pointed me towards time series models as a simpler alternative to GPs.

I'm confused. What do you mean by "time series models"? GPs can be used as time series models, too. There are some time series models which are faster in Stan than basic GP implementation with dense covariance or precision matrix.

Therefore I'm thinking that what I should do is start by implementing a time series approach, estimating the parameters of this skewnormal mixture, the fluctuation of the mixing proportion over time, and the resulting expectation and uncertainty at t+1.

Once I have this working I can see whether there is need to upgrade to using GPs. I'm thinking that because 
a) I have many data points, 
b) I am interested in a single process that evolves relatively slowly over time, and 
c) I only want to do inference relatively near my data
it might not be worth paying the price in time and complexity to upgrade to GP.

Does this seem like a sensible approach, considering what I want and the computational issues using Stan?

Benefit of Stan is that it's easy to code the model with skew normal and mixing proportion. I guess that for your data NUTS is going to be slow (which is problem if you need to run it 10K+ times, unless you can use a computer cluster). ADVI might be fast enough, but you need to check its reliability. 

With plain skew normal the problem would be easier. INLA is fast (for certain types of dynamic models) for 1D data and has skew normal. GPstuff is fast (for certain types of dynamic models) for 1D data and adding skew normal is easy. I don't know how easy it would be implement mixture of skew normal in INLA. Adding mixture of skew normals (with time varying mixing proportion) in GPstuff or GPy could be one day of work for someone familiar with these software.
 
Aki

Many thanks again!

Jonathan
